meta.titre: Total internal reflection: critical angle, fibres and prisms

sections.contenu_markdown: When you ride at night on a road near Ebolowa, the small red plastic reflectors on the back of bicycles and trucks shine back at the headlights of your car. Doctors in the hospital in Limbe use a thin glass thread to look inside a patient's body, and the internet cable reaching your town carries messages as light inside glass fibres. All of them rely on total internal reflection, a favourite GCE topic because it asks for one definition, two conditions, one short calculation and one application.

items: Light changes direction when it goes from one transparent material to another, and this is called refraction.
The angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are measured from the normal, the line at right angles to the surface.
The refractive index of a material is $n=\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}$ for light entering it from air.

sections.titre: Total internal reflection, the critical angle and sin C = 1/n
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Total internal reflection (TIR)** is the complete reflection of a ray of light back into the denser medium when it meets the boundary with a less dense medium at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle. No light is refracted out.

**Two conditions for TIR:**

1. The light must travel from a **denser medium to a less dense medium** (for example glass to air, or water to air).
2. The **angle of incidence** in the denser medium must be **greater than the critical angle** $C$.

**The critical angle** is the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the less dense medium is $90^\circ$ (the refracted ray travels along the boundary).

**Finding $C$.** Light going from air into the material obeys $n=\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}$. By reversibility, for a ray going from the material to air, the angle of incidence is $C$ and the angle of refraction is $90^\circ$, so $n=\dfrac{\sin 90^\circ}{\sin C}$, and

$$\sin C=\frac{1}{n}$$

The larger the refractive index, the smaller the critical angle. Typical values: glass ($n=1.5$) $C\approx42^\circ$; water ($n=1.33$) $C\approx49^\circ$.

**Summary of what happens at the boundary (dense to less dense):**

| Angle of incidence $i$ | Result |
|---|---|
| $i<C$ | part refracted away from the normal, part weakly reflected |
| $i=C$ | refracted ray along the boundary ($90^\circ$) |
| $i>C$ | total internal reflection, with angle of reflection $=i$ |

Always measure angles from the **normal**, not from the surface.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked how light travels along a glass thread or why it does not escape.
variantes.contenu_markdown: An optical fibre is a very thin strand of glass. Light entering one end strikes the inside wall at an angle larger than the critical angle, so it is totally internally reflected again and again along the fibre, even when the fibre is bent, until it leaves at the other end. Uses: **endoscopes** to look inside the body without surgery, **telephone and internet cables** (little energy lost, so signals travel far), and decorative lamps.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When light enters a $45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$ prism, as in periscopes, binoculars and bicycle reflectors.
variantes.contenu_markdown: A ray entering the face of a $45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$ glass prism at right angles is not bent. It hits the long face at $45^\circ$, which is greater than $C\approx42^\circ$ for glass, so it is totally reflected and turned through $90^\circ$. If it enters the long face it is reflected twice and returns parallel to the original path, turned through $180^\circ$. Prisms are used instead of mirrors because the reflection is total and the image stays bright and sharp.

sections.enonce_markdown:
The critical angle of a transparent plastic for light going from the plastic into air is $40^\circ$.

(a) Calculate the refractive index of the plastic.

(b) A ray inside the plastic reaches the plastic-air boundary at $50^\circ$ to the normal. What happens to it? What happens if the angle is $30^\circ$?

(c) A ray enters at right angles one short face of a right-angled isosceles prism made of this plastic. Will it be totally reflected at the long face?

etapes.action: Use $\sin C=1/n$ to find the refractive index.
etapes.justification: The critical angle is given, so rearrange for $n$.
TIR needs the angle of incidence to be greater than the critical angle.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $50^\circ>40^\circ$, so the ray is **totally internally reflected** and returns into the plastic at $50^\circ$.

etapes.justification: When the angle is smaller than $C$ most of the light leaves the plastic.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $30^\circ<40^\circ$, so the ray is refracted into the air, away from the normal. From $\sin r=n\sin i=1.56\times\sin30^\circ=0.78$, the angle in air is about $51^\circ$.

etapes.action: Find the angle of incidence on the long face.
etapes.justification: A ray entering a face at right angles is not deviated, and the two equal angles of the prism are $45^\circ$.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The ray meets the long face at $45^\circ$ to the normal.

etapes.justification: The ray goes from plastic to air and $45^\circ>40^\circ$.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Total internal reflection occurs, so the ray is turned through $90^\circ$.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **(a)** $n=1.56$. **(b)** At $50^\circ$ the ray is totally reflected; at $30^\circ$ it is refracted out into air. **(c)** Yes, the ray is totally reflected at the long face because $45^\circ>40^\circ$.

items.erreur_markdown: “Total internal reflection happens when light goes from air into glass at a large angle.”
items.pourquoi_faux: Light going from a less dense to a denser medium always refracts into it, bending towards the normal. TIR is possible only when the light starts in the denser medium.
items.correction_markdown: TIR needs light travelling from glass (denser) to air (less dense) with an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle.

items.pourquoi_faux: A sine can never be greater than 1. The formula is inverted.

items.erreur_markdown: Measuring the angle of incidence between the ray and the surface of the glass.
items.pourquoi_faux: All angles in reflection and refraction are measured from the normal. An angle taken from the surface is $90^\circ$ minus the true angle.
items.correction_markdown: Draw the normal first, then measure $i$ between the ray and the normal.

items.erreur_markdown: “At exactly the critical angle the ray is totally reflected.”
items.pourquoi_faux: At $i=C$ the refracted ray just skims along the boundary at $90^\circ$. Total reflection needs $i>C$.
items.correction_markdown: For $i=C$: refracted angle $=90^\circ$. For $i>C$: total internal reflection.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) State the two conditions needed for total internal reflection.

(b) A crystal has a refractive index of $2.0$. Calculate its critical angle in air.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) (1) The light travels from a **denser** to a **less dense** medium. (2) The angle of incidence in the denser medium is **greater than the critical angle**.

(b) $\sin C=\dfrac{1}{n}=\dfrac{1}{2.0}=0.50$, so $C=$ **$30^\circ$**.

items.enonce_markdown:
A designer wants a right-angled prism that turns a ray through $90^\circ$ by total internal reflection, the ray entering a short face at right angles. She can use glass with $n=1.50$ or a clear plastic with $n=1.40$.

(a) Calculate the critical angle for each material.

(b) Which material works? Explain.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Glass: $\sin C=\dfrac{1}{1.50}=0.667$, so $C=$ **$41.8^\circ$**.

Plastic: $\sin C=\dfrac{1}{1.40}=0.714$, so $C=$ **$45.6^\circ$**.

(b) The ray meets the long face at $45^\circ$. For glass, $45^\circ>41.8^\circ$, so there is total internal reflection and the glass prism works. For the plastic, $45^\circ<45.6^\circ$, so some light escapes; this prism does **not** give total reflection.

items.enonce_markdown:
A ray of light inside a glass block ($n=1.50$) reaches the glass-air boundary.

(a) Calculate the critical angle.

(b) The angle of incidence is $35^\circ$. Calculate the angle at which the ray leaves into the air.

(c) The angle of incidence is increased to $45^\circ$. Show by calculation that no light can leave the glass.

(d) Explain how this idea lets a thin glass fibre guide light around a bend.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\sin C=\dfrac{1}{1.50}=0.667$, so $C=$ **$41.8^\circ$**.

(b) $35^\circ<C$, so the ray emerges. For glass to air, $\sin r=n\sin i=1.50\times\sin35^\circ=1.50\times0.574=0.860$, so $r=$ **$59.4^\circ$** (away from the normal).

(c) Trying the same formula gives $\sin r=1.50\times\sin45^\circ=1.50\times0.707=1.06$. A sine cannot exceed 1, so there is no refracted ray: the light is **totally internally reflected**, as expected since $45^\circ>41.8^\circ$.

(d) Light enters the fibre almost along its axis and meets the wall at an angle greater than $C$, so it is totally reflected and stays inside; at each bend it is reflected again, so it follows the fibre until it reaches the end.

items_markdown: Total internal reflection: all the light is reflected back into the denser medium at the boundary with a less dense medium.
Two conditions: light going from a denser to a less dense medium, and angle of incidence greater than the critical angle.
Critical angle: $\sin C=\dfrac{1}{n}$; glass $\approx42^\circ$, water $\approx49^\circ$. At $i=C$ the refracted ray is at $90^\circ$.
Measure all angles from the normal; a sine can never exceed 1.
Uses: optical fibres (endoscopes, communication cables), right-angled prisms (periscopes, binoculars, bicycle reflectors).
